assessment.title: Advanced DSA Diagnostic Assessment
assessment.description: 35 multiple-choice questions covering harder algorithmic concepts, complexity analysis, and problem-solving.

questions.text: Find the single element that appears once while all others appear three times, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The standard technique is:
options: Bit-by-bit counting modulo 3 with two bitmasks
questions.explanation: At each bit position the count is either a multiple of 3 or 3k+1 (the unique element); two masks (ones/twos) implement this in constant space.

questions.text: The 'trapping rain water' problem on an array of column heights can be solved in O(n) time using:
options: Two pointers with running left-max and right-max
questions.explanation: Move the pointer on the side with the smaller running maximum; the trapped water at that column is determined by the smaller of the two maxima.

questions.text: For finding the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array of n elements, the best average-case complexity available is:
options: O(n), by Quickselect (average case, O(n^2) worst)
questions.explanation: Quickselect achieves expected O(n) time, though worst case remains O(n^2) without median-of-medians.

questions.text: The minimum time to decide whether t is an anagram of s (both length n, lowercase English) is:
options: O(n log n), by sorting both strings
questions.explanation: A single pass builds a frequency count of size 26 and a second pass verifies.

questions.text: The key idea of the Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching algorithm is:
options: Precomputing a failure/prefix table to skip redundant comparisons
Sorting the characters of the pattern
Binary searching the text for the pattern's first character
questions.explanation: The failure function records the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, letting the search resume without backtracking.

questions.text: Building a suffix array for a length-n string using the doubling algorithm with radix sort at each level runs in:
questions.explanation: Doubling is O(n log n) rounds with each round sorting in O(n) using radix sort (comparison-sort versions are O(n log^2 n)).

questions.text: Which approach sorts an array of all-equal keys in O(n) time and is stable?
questions.explanation: 3-way partitioning detects all-equal subarrays and returns immediately, giving O(n).

questions.text: The time complexity of searching a target in a rotated sorted array (with all distinct elements) is:
questions.explanation: At each step one half is sorted; that half can be searched by an ordinary binary-search comparison, keeping total time O(log n).

questions.text: External merge sort must sort a file of N pages when M pages of main memory are available. Its I/O complexity (ignoring constants) is:
questions.explanation: The initial run generation is O(N), and each subsequent merge pass is a factor; the total number of passes is roughly log_{M-1}(N/M).

questions.text: The worst-case time complexity of the median-of-medians selection algorithm for the k-th smallest element is:
questions.explanation: The median-of-medians pivot guarantees at least a constant fraction of the array is discarded each level, giving T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) = O(n).

questions.text: Deleting a given node in a doubly linked list when you already hold a pointer to that node takes:
questions.explanation: Because prev and next are directly accessible from the node, only local pointer updates are needed.

questions.text: To both detect a cycle and return its entry node in O(n) time and O(1) space, you should:
options: Use a hash set of visited nodes
After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both by one until they meet again
questions.explanation: The meeting point plus the head-distance argument yields the cycle entry in a second linear pass.

questions.text: Given two singly linked lists that converge into a Y shape, the intersection node can be found in O(m+n) time and O(1) space by:
options: Hashing all nodes of the first list
Two pointers that traverse both lists by switching heads on completion
questions.explanation: Advancing each pointer over both lists equalises the lengths, so they meet at the intersection node in at most m+n steps.

questions.text: Reversing a singly linked list in groups of k with O(1) extra space has which time complexity in terms of n, the number of nodes?
questions.explanation: Every node is visited a constant number of times (once inside its group's reversal), so total time is O(n) for any fixed k.

questions.text: The Towers of Hanoi with n disks requires how many moves (and hence how much recursive time)?
questions.explanation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 solves to 2^n - 1 moves.

questions.text: Which of these recursive algorithms uses O(log n) call-stack depth on its typical input?
options: Post-order traversal of a balanced binary tree
Linear recursion over a linked list
questions.explanation: A balanced tree has height O(log n), so the deepest recursion stack is O(log n) frames.

questions.text: A recursive function calls itself twice per level with input size n/2, doing O(n) work per level. Its time complexity is:
questions.explanation: By the master theorem, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is case 2, giving Theta(n log n).

questions.text: Applying memoisation to the exponential recursive Fibonacci reduces its cost to:
options: O(log n) time and O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each of the n subproblems is computed once and cached, so time is linear and the cache is linear.

questions.text: Which statement about tail recursion is FALSE?
options: The recursive call is the last operation in the function body
With TCO, tail recursion uses O(1) stack space
Every recursive function can be trivially rewritten as a tail-recursive one without an accumulator
With TCO, tail recursion is essentially equivalent to a loop
questions.explanation: Non-tail recursions such as naive Fibonacci cannot be made tail-recursive without a substantial restructuring, typically involving an accumulator or continuation.

questions.text: In a binary search tree, the in-order successor of a node that has a right subtree is:
options: The leftmost node of its right subtree
The rightmost node of its left subtree
questions.explanation: The smallest key greater than the node is the minimum of its right subtree.

questions.text: The height of a complete binary tree with n nodes is:
questions.explanation: A complete tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1)-1 nodes, so h = O(log n).

questions.text: Inserting n keys in strictly increasing order into a plain (unbalanced) BST gives a search time of:
questions.explanation: Sorted insertion produces a degenerate chain whose height is n, so a search is O(n).

questions.text: The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (root at level 0) is:
The time complexity of computing a binary tree's diameter (longest path between any two nodes) using a single depth-first pass is:
questions.explanation: Each node computes its height once and updates a global maximum, giving O(n).

questions.text: The maximum height of a red-black tree with n internal nodes is:
questions.explanation: The red-black invariants imply h <= 2 log2(n+1), so height is O(log n).

questions.text: Building a min-heap of n unordered elements with the bottom-up heapify algorithm runs in:
questions.explanation: Most nodes sit near the leaves and sift down a short distance; the total work is Theta(n) even though each sift is O(log n).

questions.text: In the 0/1 knapsack DP table dp[i][w], what does the entry represent?
options: The maximum value achievable using the first i items with capacity w
Whether item i fits in capacity w
The number of items whose weight is at most w
The minimum weight to achieve value i
questions.explanation: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], value_i + dp[i-1][w-weight_i]) for weight_i <= w.

questions.text: The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) can be solved in which pair of complexities?
options: O(n^2) by simple DP, and O(n log n) by patience sorting with binary search
questions.explanation: The classic O(n^2) DP and the O(n log n) patience/binary-search variant are both standard.

questions.text: The edit distance (Levenshtein) between "kitten" and "sitting" is:
questions.explanation: k→s, e→i, and inserting g at the end give a total cost of 3.

questions.text: The length of the longest palindromic subsequence of "BBABCBCAB" is:
questions.explanation: "BABCBAB" is a palindromic subsequence of length 7.

questions.text: For matrices with dimensions [10, 30, 5, 60], the minimum number of scalar multiplications in the optimal parenthesisation is:
Compared with longest common subsequence, the DP for longest common substring requires that:
options: An extra third dimension be added for length
dp[i][j] tracks a contiguous match ending at positions i and j, and the answer is the max of dp[i][j] rather than the last cell
No change is needed; the two problems are identical
questions.explanation: LCS uses a suffix-style recurrence; LCSubstring resets dp[i][j] to 0 on mismatch and takes the maximum over the table.

questions.text: Wildcard pattern matching with pattern length m and text length n, using the standard DP, has time complexity:
questions.explanation: The table has m*n states, each computed in O(1).

questions.text: The DP for regular-expression matching with '.' and '*' (pattern length m, text length n) has time complexity:
questions.explanation: Each of the m*n states is filled in O(1), because '*' expands to two transitions rather than iterating over lengths.

questions.text: In the O(n^2) DP for longest palindromic substring, dp[i][j] represents:
options: The length of the longest palindrome in s[i..j]
The longest common prefix of s[i..] and reverse(s[j..])
The number of palindromic substrings of s[i..j]
questions.explanation: The recurrence dp[i][j] = (s[i]==s[j]) AND (j-i<2 OR dp[i+1][j-1]) records a palindrome-or-not boolean.
